text: Two people meet again in a police station; when they last saw each other, she was a housemaid and he was about to become a soldier. Kim Ho-sun builds the film out of that gap — the years a young woman spends inside other people's houses, on wages that never accumulate — and the romance supplies only a shape, a courtship recalled, while an economy grinds underneath it. What has happened to Yeong-ja happened because of where she worked and who owned the house, and the film states this flatly, keeping her at eye level instead of at the height of pity. The KOFA 100 keeps it, and the reason is the accounting rather than the tears. It opens not with the couple but with the state, which meets her as a case.

Fog does the plotting: a man of title takes a wrong turning, walks into the wrong dinner party, and is handed a tray. Sixty-seven minutes is as long as that misunderstanding lasts, and Alfred E. Green spends them on a nobleman who could end it at any moment by giving his own name, and does not. In 1930 a comedy still had to prove that talk could carry it, which suits a premise where everything hangs on who may speak and in what tone. The National Board of Review put it among the ten best films of that year, an odd berth for a farce built from one door and one wrong assumption. The class joke is not subtle, and does not need to be: the whole house has agreed to see a uniform instead of a face.

Eddie Warmack comes out of prison with his playing intact and no intention of renting it out. That refusal is the plot: the clubs and the studios belong to men who did not make the music, a saxophonist who will not sign has nowhere to play, and so he goes looking for his grandfather instead — Poppa Harris, a musician old enough to know when the arrangement was made. Larry Clark films the search rather than a career, which lets the thing move by association, a room and a rehearsal and a face recalled, closer to a solo than to a story. Jazz here is never atmosphere. The National Film Registry holds the film. What it argues about is ownership: who holds the tape, who collects on it, and what a musician gives up to stay in the room where the sound is made.

The wedding happens early, which leaves the rest of the film for the marriage. Lee Myung-se takes two people who fell in love at college and married on schedule, then watches agreement turn out to have been a phase: they quarrel over nothing in particular, and each nothing is staged as an event. A comedy that begins after the ceremony has to find its material in furniture and habit, and this one is alert to how fast a misreading hardens — a wife waiting in a coffee shop, a husband arriving to find her with a man he cannot place, a whole afternoon of private theatre built on a wrong guess. It is on the KOFA 100 list of Korean films. Jealousy in this marriage is less a wound than a pastime, and the film is funny about that without excusing either of them.

Home movies of a wealthy American family, cut against frames painted by hand: that is the material Jerome Hill had, and Film Portrait is what he made from it. Eighty minutes of a man assembling himself out of footage shot of him as a child by relatives and footage he shot decades later in an entirely different idiom, surreal where the family reels are dutiful. The premise underneath is odd — that one life ran alongside the medium recording it, so that the memoir and the history of the form come off the same shelf. The National Film Registry preserves it. This is not an illustrated account: the images existed first and the telling was fitted to them, which is why the film can let a passage stay pure colour and decline to explain itself.

Two hundred and eighty minutes, issued a chapter at a time, every chapter built to make the following week feel necessary. An insurance company president is killed by a cloaked figure known only by his hand, and it is his daughter — not the police, not a lawyer — who goes out and hires the detective, a man whose method is laboratory apparatus rather than hunches. The 1914 serial ran on that arrangement: a heroine who initiates, a villain kept faceless so he can be anyone at the table, a crisis at the close of each instalment that has to be paid off in the first shot of the next. The National Film Registry keeps it. Watching it now means watching the mechanism work, which is no loss, since the mechanism was the attraction: suspense sold on a weekly schedule, with the schedule showing.

In 1967 a group of Philadelphia teenagers made a film about the gang they were in, and it runs twenty-two minutes. Part of it is documentary and part is reenactment, and the seam between them is the interesting place: a boy playing himself at a distance of weeks, deciding what a camera needs to see. Nothing has been arranged for a visitor. The explanations of territory, of who is owed what, come from inside and are addressed as much to the members as to anyone watching, which gives the short a double register, record and rehearsal at once. In 1968 it took the Documentary Film Award at the Festival de Popoli in Italy, an unlikely journey for something shot on a few blocks by people still in their teens.

A French prisoner and the daughter of the German officer who keeps him: the arrangement is old, and both of them know it. William K. Howard has sixty-nine minutes and a Pierre Benoit novel, Axelle, to compress, so the courtship proceeds mostly in the grammar of who is permitted to speak first and who must pretend not to have heard. The war it draws on was recent enough in 1931 that nobody in the audience needed the map explained, and that changes the temperature of a romance between enemies: sympathy is not a gesture here, it costs something on both sides. The National Board of Review named it one of the ten best films of the year. What holds up is the awkwardness — two people negotiating affection in a borrowed language, under supervision, on someone else's schedule.

The voice is Orson Welles's, which is a decision before it is a credit: a public life handed to a narrator who cannot help sounding like a proclamation. The Finest Hours runs 116 minutes and works from two incompatible materials — newsreel of things a camera happened to catch, and scenes built in 1964 to stand where no camera was — and it cuts between them freely. Attention drifts to the joins. Which shot is evidence, which is illustration, and whether the film thinks the difference matters: those questions run alongside the biography and are livelier than it is. It took the Academy Award for best documentary feature. Churchill is the subject, but the demonstration is what happens to a career once it is read aloud at that pitch.

One of them arrives with a past and the other with nothing but the present, and the film runs on that imbalance. A man and a woman fall for each other; her history with men keeps entering the room, so the love story is continually interrupted by people who are not there. Lee Jang-ho gives it a hundred and ten minutes, long enough that the affection stops being a device and becomes a condition the two of them live inside. Melodrama shaped this way has to decide whether the woman's past counts as explanation or as charge, and that decision is the real subject. It is on the KOFA 100. What gets examined is not desire so much as the residue desire leaves in someone who has been through it more than once.

The camp is in the mountains, and the film never comes down. Piagol stays inside a communist guerrilla band where food is short and suspicion is plentiful, and where the presence of one woman among the men rearranges every hierarchy the unit believed it had. Nothing is fought at scale here. The war arrives as rumour and as rations, and the tension comes from a man who has decided to leave and must first work out who would report him. Made in 1955, for an audience that had just lived those years from the other side of the line, it takes the risk of granting the enemy boredom and jealousy and fear instead of doctrine. The KOFA 100 has kept it in view. The mountain does the rest of the work: cold, steep, indifferent to whose side anyone is on.

Beautiful hair, by the standard the advertisements set, is hair that lifts when the wind hits it. Ayoka Chenzira treats that standard as a technical specification and spends ten animated minutes on the equipment sold to meet it: relaxer, gel, curler, comb, each introduced with the brightness of a commercial and the timing of a joke. Drawing helps — a line can take a chemical burn that a person would have to survive — and the narration stays light while the arithmetic of money and hours piles up beneath it. The short has become a fixture of classroom argument about race and images, which is weight for ten minutes to carry cheerfully. The National Film Registry holds it. The mockery is aimed at the standard throughout, and never at the women keeping to it.

Nurses on horseback, on mountain roads that will not take a car. The Frontier Nursing Service is both the subject and the reason for the film, which gives 59 minutes to the plain logistics of medicine in the Appalachians: the creek forded, the saddlebag opened, the cabin reached after dark. Some of it is staged so that a case can be followed rather than an agency described, which puts the picture between record and argument and makes it franker than either. Terrain is what it documents best. The mountains are not scenery but the explanation for why the service takes this form, why the medicine travels instead of the patient. The National Film Registry keeps it, and what stays legible is the work: one household at a time, at the speed of a horse.

A women's club in Wisconsin Dells sits through a lecture on the Soviet threat, falls asleep, and wakes on a collective farm. Miriam Bennett made this in 1932 and it lasts eighteen minutes, in which the Tuesday Club's members are both the drowsy audience in the hall and the labourers toiling under the eye of the special police. The joke therefore cuts two ways at once, at the alarmism of the lecture and at the comfort of the women listening to it, and the film never quite says which target it prefers. Its resources are a room, a nap and a costume box. The National Film Registry took it in, a fair outcome for a picture made outside any studio by people who cast themselves as their own worst nightmare and found it funny.
